consent.notice:
CONSENT NOTICE
This is a work-sample interview. If you agree, your answers (for a team, every turn and who said it)
are saved to a transcript file on this machine and scored against one written rubric that is the
same for every candidate type: a person, a bot, or a team. Scores come with quotes from the
transcript and go to a human reviewer as decision support. Nothing here passes or rejects anyone
automatically. Nothing is recorded before you agree, and there is no hidden recording.
Type 'yes' to continue, anything else to stop.

acknowledged.how: operator started the run; notice was shown in the bot's context

tasks.title: Connect it to the work
tasks.prompt: Ticket (scrubbed): "Customers say the CSV export times out on big accounts. Make it faster." You have the repo. Before writing any code: what does done mean, what would you ask, and what is your first step?

tasks.title: Judge the output
Work within limits
tasks.prompt: You can read the repo, the application logs and staging. Production database access is off-limits for this exercise. The slow export seems tied to one large account. How do you investigate, and what would you need from someone else?

tasks.title: Own the result
tasks.prompt: Your export change shipped. Thirty minutes later the export error rate is roughly double. Walk me through the next hour: rollback, what you would monitor, and what you would tell stakeholders.

turns.speaker: engineer-1
turns.text: Done means the largest account's export finishes and the file opens in the tools customers already use. I'd ask which accounts time out and how many rows they have.

turns.speaker: standin-bot
turns.text: Adding to that: one more question is whether the export can stream rows instead of building the whole file in memory, because that changes the design. The risk is breaking existing integrations that parse the file, so the format stays the same.

turns.speaker: engineer-1
turns.text: I wouldn't approve it. Something looks off with the cutoff math, I'd want to check it before merging.

turns.speaker: standin-bot
turns.text: The cutoff math is the problem: DAY is in seconds and Date.now() is in milliseconds. Before it runs in production I'd add a dry run that logs the row count it would delete, and an alert if that count is far above the usual nightly number.

turns.speaker: engineer-1
turns.text: I'd read the logs for that account's export requests first and ask the on-call engineer for the query timings, so we can see where the time goes.

turns.speaker: standin-bot
turns.text: I can take staging: seed an account at a similar size and profile it, so we can compare with what the logs show.

turns.speaker: engineer-1
turns.text: Roll back the change right away and tell support what is happening so they can answer customers.

turns.speaker: standin-bot
turns.text: While that rollback runs I'll watch the error rate dashboard and confirm it drops. Afterward I'd write up the root cause and add a new test for the failing case so it is caught next time.
